unit.title: Subjunctive with Advanced Conjunctions
unit.subtitle: Conjunctions that always take the subjunctive, plus future time clauses

grammar.title: Some conjunctions never let you use the indicative
grammar.intro: A handful of conjunctions are hard-wired to the subjunctive: they point to a purpose, a condition, or something not yet real, so the indicative simply never follows them. A second group — the time conjunctions like cuando and en cuanto — flip to the subjunctive only when the action is still in the future. Master both and your subjunctive will finally sound automatic.

sections.heading: Conjunctions that ALWAYS take the subjunctive
sections.body: These express purpose or condition about something unrealised, so they always trigger the subjunctive. Learn them as a fixed set — no exceptions:
conj: para que / a fin de que

ex.es: Lo haré con tal de que me ayudes.
ex.en: I'll do it provided that you help me.
I'll call you before you leave.

sections.heading: Purpose and condition in action
sections.body: Notice how each conjunction frames something that hasn't happened yet — a goal, a proviso, a precaution. That unreality is exactly why the subjunctive appears:

ex.es: En caso de que llueva, quédate en casa.
ex.en: In case it rains, stay home.
He left without anyone seeing him.

sections.heading: Time conjunctions: subjunctive for the future
sections.body: Cuando, en cuanto, tan pronto como, hasta que, mientras take the indicative for habits or the past, but the subjunctive when the action is still ahead of you:

ex.en: I'll call you as soon as I arrive.

takeaways: Always subjunctive: a fin de que, con tal de que, a menos que, en caso de que, sin que, antes de que, para que.
Time conjunctions (cuando, en cuanto, tan pronto como, hasta que, mientras) → subjunctive for a future action.
Same time words + a habit or the past → indicative: Cuando llego, como. / Cuando llegué, comí.
Lo haré con tal de que me ayudes; En caso de que llueva, quédate.

mistakes.why: The arrival is still in the future, so the time clause needs the subjunctive: llegue.

mistakes.w: Lo haré con tal de que me ayudas.
mistakes.r: Lo haré con tal de que me ayudes.
mistakes.why: Con tal de que always takes the subjunctive: ayudes.

mistakes.w: En caso de que llueve, quédate.
mistakes.r: En caso de que llueva, quédate.
mistakes.why: En caso de que always takes the subjunctive: llueva.

exercises.prompt: Lo haré con tal de que me ___. (ayudar, tú)
exercises.prompt_en: I'll do it provided that you help me.
exercises.no: Con tal de que always takes the subjunctive: “ayudes”.

exercises.prompt_en: I'll call you as soon as I arrive.
exercises.no: The arrival is still in the future, so use the subjunctive: “llegue”.

exercises.prompt: Build: “In case it rains, stay home.”
exercises.no: “En caso de que llueva, quédate en casa” — this conjunction needs the subjunctive.
The action is still ahead, so use the subjunctive: “termine”.

exercises.prompt: Match each conjunction to its meaning.

exercises.tts: No iré a menos que vengas conmigo.
accepted: no ire a menos que vengas conmigo
exercises.translation: I won't go unless you come with me.
exercises.ok: ¡Correcto! “No iré a menos que vengas conmigo.”
exercises.no: It was: “No iré a menos que vengas conmigo.” (I won't go unless you come with me.)

exercises.scenario: Making plans with a friend for tonight 🌙

options.text: Te aviso tan pronto como salga del trabajo.
Te aviso tan pronto como salgo del trabajo.
Te aviso tan pronto como saldré del trabajo.

exercises.no: Leaving work is still in the future, so use the subjunctive: “tan pronto como salga”.

exercises.en: I'll call you as soon as I arrive.
exercises.no: Almost — tap “Hear it”, then match the sound of “Te llamo en cuanto llegue.”
